481	174          In our study, defensive linemen accounted for the largest proportion of players
482	
483	175   undergoing surgical repair of distal biceps tears (11/25). Defensive players overall represented
484	
485	176   76% of all cases. We propose that the higher rate of injury among defensive players, and
486	
487	177   defensive lineman in particular, is due to the fact that their arm is placed in a position at risk for
488	
489	178   an eccentric contraction of the biceps as the extremity is forced from a flexed to extended
490	
491	179   position, particularly when fighting through a block or making a tackle. We believe offensive
492	
493	180   lineman to be at increased risk for similar reasons. Of note, offensive lineman were the only
494

504	182          There are several significant limitations to our study that deserve attention. First, using
505	
506	183   publicly available data to identify distal biceps tendon surgical repair is prone to selection,
507	
508	184   reporting, and observer bias. The use of publicly available data limits the capability to define
509	
510	185   injury severity and the specific surgical procedure and technique performed. Details such as past
511	
512	186   medical and surgical history, surgical technique, and rehab protocols were not available for
513	
514	187   collection. Additionally, the sample analyzed in this study may underrepresent the true number
515	
516	188   of cases that occurred over this 20-year period due to the nature of data collection using publicly
517	
518	189   available information. The time to return to sport reported in this study is largely dependent on
519	
520	190   the point in the season at which the injury occurred, making it difficult to draw conclusions from
521	
522	191   this information. We could not control for potential cofounders including concomitant injuries,
523	
524	192   trades, personal obligations, coaching changes, or changes in offensive and defensive systems
525	
526	193   that may have impacted both the case and control cohorts. We must stress that these factors
527	
528	194   likely confound the findings of decreased post-injury career length and games per season
529	
530	195   reported in our study, and these results should be interpreted with caution. Furthermore, we
531	
532	196   could not control for compliance with treatment and rehab protocols. Additional limitations
533	
534	197   include incomplete follow-up and career length analysis for players still in the NFL. Lastly, we
535	
536	198   are unable to evaluate offensive linemen with performance scoring.

541	
542	201          In this study, we aimed to determine whether surgical repair of distal biceps tendon
543	
544	202   ruptures in National Football League players would lead to a decrease in post-injury performance
545	
546	203   and to define return to sport, post-injury career length, and games played per season following
547	
548	204   injury. In our analysis, 84% of NFL players were able to return to sport following distal biceps

558	
559	206   performance when compared to the player’s pre-injury performance and control-matched peers,
560	
561	207   in those athletes that were able to return to play. NFL players who underwent surgical repair of
562	
563	208   the distal biceps tendon played fewer games per season compared with matched controls,
564	
565	209   although this finding is likely influenced by a number of factors we could not control for. Players
566

568

      Distal Biceps Ruptures in NFL Athletes


1    Abstract

2    Background: The purpose of this study was to determine whether surgical repair of distal biceps

3    tendon ruptures in professional football players would lead to a decrease in post-injury

4    performance when compared to pre-injury performance and control-matched peers. We also

5    sought to define return to sport, post-injury career length, and games played per season in

6    National Football League players following surgical repair of distal biceps tendon ruptures.

7    Methods: Data for National Football League players who underwent surgical repair of distal

8    biceps tendon ruptures during a 20-year time period were collected. 25 cases in 22 players were

9    included in the analysis. Matched controls based on player position, age, experience, and

10   performance statistics were identified. Performance scores for cases and controls were calculated

11   using a standardized scoring system specific to player position.

12   Results: Of the 25 cases, 21 (84%) were able to return to sport in the National Football League.

13   The overall 1-year survival rate of return to play in players undergoing surgical repair of distal

14   biceps tendon ruptures was 76% and overall 2-year survival was 56%. Players who underwent

15   surgical repair of distal biceps tendon ruptures had significantly shorter post-injury career lengths

16   and played fewer games per season post-injury than matched controls. There was no significant

17   difference by position in post-injury performance scores when compared to matched controls.


18   Conclusion: National Football League players undergoing surgical repair of distal biceps tendon

19   ruptures have a high rate of return to sport, though many retire within the next few seasons

20   following surgery. Players who do return to competition can be expected to perform at a level

21   comparable to their peers.


22   Level of Evidence: Level IV; Case Series; Treatment Study




                                                                                                          1
      Distal Biceps Ruptures in NFL Athletes


23   Keywords: distal biceps, biceps tear, return to sport, return to play, NFL, football, sports injuries


24


25

26          Distal biceps tendon ruptures account for three to ten percent of all biceps injuries with

27   an incidence of 1.2 per 100,000 persons per year.14,17 The vast majority of these injuries occur in

28   the dominant extremity of men, with more than half occurring in patients in their thirties. In

29   active patients, surgical repair is recommended to restore elbow flexion strength (30%

30   improvement), supination strength (40% improvement), and upper extremity endurance.3

31          National Football League (NFL) players are routinely exposed to high physical demands,

32   predisposing these athletes to higher injury rates than any other sport.4 Surgical treatment of

33   various upper extremity injuries, such as forearm and clavicle fracture repair, can negatively

34   impact return to sport, post-injury performance, and overall career length in NFL players.11,15

35   However, there is a paucity of literature regarding return to play and performance after distal

36   biceps repair, and to date, there are no known studies examining these outcomes in NFL athletes.

37          The purpose of this study was to evaluate player performance before and after injury in

38   NFL players who underwent distal biceps tendon repair while controlling for the performance of

39   these athletes with uninjured, matched-controls. We also aimed to define return to sport, post-

40   injury career length, and games played per season in NFL players following surgical repair of

41   distal biceps tendon ruptures. We hypothesized that NFL players who underwent surgical repair

42   of the distal biceps would have a significantly shorter post-injury career length and fewer games

43   played per season compared with matched controls. Furthermore, we hypothesized that surgical

44   repair of the distal biceps would lead to a decrease in performance when compared to the




                                                                                                         2
      Distal Biceps Ruptures in NFL Athletes


45   player’s pre-injury performance and control-matched peers, in those athletes that were able to

46   return to play.

47

48   Materials and Methods

49           This case series contained NFL players who underwent surgical repair of distal biceps

50   tendon ruptures during a 20-year time period between the 1998 and 2017 seasons. Subjects were

51   identified using a comprehensive online injury database (www.prosportstransactions.com) cross-

52   referenced with team press releases, online injury reports, and player profiles (www.nfl.com and

53   www.pro-football-reference.com). This methodology has been validated in multiple studies

54   across multiple sports.1,2,4,5,6,9,10,11,13,15,16 Given the public nature of this data, this study was

55   exempt from Institutional Review Board approval and did not require informed consent.

56           Twenty-eight cases of distal biceps tendon ruptures in twenty-six players were initially

57   identified. All cases were treated with surgery. Players were included for analysis if they had

58   played in at least one NFL season before the index injury season. Of the twenty-eight cases, 3

59   were in players in their first year in the league and were excluded due to lack of performance

60   data prior to the injury. The remaining twenty-five players had complete statistical performance

61   data and were included in the study cohort.

62           A one-to-one matched control group was selected based upon similarity scores provided

63   by a comprehensive online database (www.pro-football-reference.com). These scores identify

64   players whose careers are most similar according to performance data and seasons of play.

65   Players in the control cohort were additionally matched according to position and all efforts were

66   made to select controls without a significant injury history. A cohort group was utilized for

67   comparison to minimize potential confounding variables inherent in the career path of NFL




                                                                                                              3
      Distal Biceps Ruptures in NFL Athletes


68   players as their performance may be affected by increasing age and experience. Controls were

69   matched both to the age of the study subject (+/- 1 year) and career experience (+/- 1 year) at the

70   time of surgery. For subjects, the index injury season was defined as the season in which the

71   player underwent surgery. Matched controls were assigned an index date or time, which matched

72   the injured subject’s surgery date relative to their career experience. For example, if a 28 year-

73   old player underwent surgery 3 years into his career, a matched control was chosen who was also

74   28 years-old at an index date 3 years into his career.

75          Return to sport data was collected for all players included in the analysis. Return to sport

76   was defined as play in any single NFL game following surgery. A player did not return to sport if

77   he did not play in any NFL game after surgery. A Kaplan-Meier survivorship curve with final

78   game played as the endpoint was created post-injury for cases and post-index for controls.

79          Demographic data, including player age, position, career experience, and date of surgery

80   were recorded. Performance data, from regular season games only, was recorded for players

81   before and after surgery using www.pro-football-reference.com. Performance statistics were also

82   recorded for controls pre- and post-index. Each statistical category was divided by games played

83   to account for discrepancies in number of games played per season. A player’s performance

84   score was then calculated using a previously published and standardized scoring system specific

85   to player position.6,10,11,15,16 (Figure 1) Statistics per game were used to calculate each

86   performance score per game. Positions without previously defined performance scores (offensive

87   lineman) were excluded from performance score analysis. This methodology has been previously

88   published in multiple studies.6,10,11,12,15,16 Post-injury performance scores, games per season, and

89   career lengths for subjects were compared to post-index performance scores, games per season,

90   and career lengths for controls relative to their index date.




                                                                                                            4
       Distal Biceps Ruptures in NFL Athletes


 91          Comparisons were made using paired-samples Student t tests with significance set at

 92   P<0.05.

 93

 94   Results

 95          Twenty-five surgeries in twenty-two players were analyzed. Average age at time of

 96   injury was 28 +/- 3.0 years and mean NFL career experience at time of surgery was 6.0 +/- 2.8

 97   years. Three players tore their contralateral distal biceps tendon following return to sport and

 98   required surgery. They were counted as two cases each. Defensive linemen accounted for the

 99   most cases (11, 44%), followed by offensive linemen (6, 24%). Together, offensive and

100   defensive linemen accounted for 68% of cases. Defensive players accounted for 76% of cases,

101   with the only offensive players sustaining injury being offensive lineman. There were no cases

102   involving offensive skill position players.

103          Twenty-one cases (84%) were able to return to sport in the NFL (Table I). 83.3% of

104   offensive players and 84.2% of defensive players were able to return to sport. Linebackers had

105   the lowest rate of return to sport (66.7%), although only three players played this position, while

106   all defensive backs were able to return to sport (100%). Mean number of days to return to sport

107   was 321 +/- 45. No players were able to return to play during the same season as injury. One

108   player was injured in the offseason and was able to return to play for the start of the following

109   season (236 days post-injury). The overall 1-year survival rate of return to play in players

110   undergoing surgical repair of distal biceps tendon rupture was 76% and overall 2-year survival

111   was 56%. (Figure 2)

112          Comparison of the case cohort with the control cohort revealed that the controls were

113   well matched pre-index as there was no significant difference in age, career experience, games




                                                                                                          5
       Distal Biceps Ruptures in NFL Athletes


114   per season, or performance scores. (Tables II, III) Players in the control group (3.4 +/- 2.0 years)

115   had a significantly longer career length post-index than players who underwent surgical

116   treatment of distal biceps tendon ruptures (2.8 +/- 2.0 years) post-injury (P=0.049). (Table IV)

117   Defensive backs who underwent surgical repair of the distal biceps had a significantly shorter

118   career length post-injury compared to controls post-index (P=0.02) (Table IV). Players in the

119   control group (13 +/- 2.3) played significantly more games per season post-index than players

120   who underwent surgical treatment of distal biceps ruptures (11 +/- 4.0) post-injury, over the

121   duration of their careers (P=0.02). (Table IV) There was no difference in games per season post-

122   injury or post-index by position. (Table IV) There was no significant difference by position in

123   post-injury performance scores when compared to post-index matched controls. (Table V)

124

125   Discussion

126          Distal biceps tendon ruptures occur secondary to an excessive eccentric tension as the

127   arm is forced from a flexed to extended position.14 Patients typically describe a painful “pop” at

128   time of injury with proximal retraction of the biceps muscle belly and weakness with forearm

129   supination.17 The unique physical demands placed on NFL athletes during game play and

130   practice make these athletes prone to this injury. Surgical repair is recommended to allow for the

131   best chance at a full return to play and performance.

132          There is a paucity of data regarding return to play and performance in athletes in any

133   sport. One prior study investigated athletes undergoing repair of distal biceps tendon ruptures.7

134   This case series analyzed just ten athletes across a range of sports (eight of which were

135   categorized as weight lifters or body builders) and their level of competition was poorly defined.

136   The authors of this study reported that “all patients returned to unlimited activities and




                                                                                                           6
       Distal Biceps Ruptures in NFL Athletes


137   experienced no pain”. However, post-injury performance was not analyzed. No other studies

138   have published on return to competitive athletic performance following surgical repair of distal

139   biceps tears. Furthermore, there is no published data assessing the effect of surgical repair of

140   distal biceps tears on future athletic performance

141          We found that 84% of NFL players undergoing surgical repair of distal biceps tendon

142   ruptures were able to return to sport (defined as play in a single NFL game). This return to sport

143   rate is lower than that reported following other upper extremity surgeries in NFL players

144   including forearm fracture repair (91.7%), clavicle fracture repair (94.1%), and thumb UCL

145   repair (95.7%).11,15,16 No players were able to return during the same season of injury.

146   Furthermore, in our study, a large number of players retired within the next few seasons

147   following surgery. One-year survival in players undergoing surgical repair of distal biceps tears

148   was 76%. At 2 years post-injury, just 56% of players undergoing surgical repair of distal biceps

149   tears remain in the NFL.

150          Our study shows that return to play at any performance level is not guaranteed, as only

151   84% of the players returned for at least one game. We also confirmed our second hypothesis, as

152   players who underwent surgical repair of distal biceps tendon ruptures had significantly shorter

153   post-injury career lengths compared with matched controls. Furthermore, players who underwent

154   surgical repair of distal biceps tendon ruptures played significantly fewer games per season post-

155   injury than matched controls. There was no significant difference in post-injury performance

156   compared to pre-injury, and no significant difference in post-injury performance compared to

157   matched controls.

158          We found that cases had a statistically significantly shorter career length following

159   surgery (2.8 years) when compared with controls (3.4 years), but it is unlikely that this difference




                                                                                                           7
       Distal Biceps Ruptures in NFL Athletes


160   is clinically significant. The average career length for all NFL players overall is 3.3 years.8 Mean

161   experience for players undergoing surgical repair of distal biceps tendon ruptures in our study

162   was 6 years, well exceeding the overall career length average. Given that the mean career

163   experience at time of injury for players in our study well exceeded the average career length of

164   NFL players overall, it is likely that these players were already towards the end of their playing

165   careers at the time of injury. Players undergoing surgical repair of distal biceps tendon ruptures

166   did play significantly fewer games per season post-surgery (11 games per season) compared to

167   matched controls (13 games per season). In our study there was no significant difference in post-

168   injury performance for cases compared to matched controls. Our data provides valuable

169   information regarding expectations for post-injury return to sport. Players undergoing distal

170   biceps tendon repair who are able to return to sport can expect to perform at a level comparable

171   to their pre-injury performance. Based on our data, a player who has this injury and undergoes

172   surgery may play in fewer games per season but is unlikely to have a shorter post-injury career

173   than their peers.

174          In our study, defensive linemen accounted for the largest proportion of players

175   undergoing surgical repair of distal biceps tears (11/25). Defensive players overall represented

176   76% of all cases. We propose that the higher rate of injury among defensive players, and

177   defensive lineman in particular, is due to the fact that their arm is placed in a position at risk for

178   an eccentric contraction of the biceps as the extremity is forced from a flexed to extended

179   position, particularly when fighting through a block or making a tackle. We believe offensive

180   lineman to be at increased risk for similar reasons. Of note, offensive lineman were the only

181   players on the offensive side of the ball to sustain this injury.




                                                                                                               8
       Distal Biceps Ruptures in NFL Athletes


182          There are several significant limitations to our study that deserve attention. First, using

183   publicly available data to identify distal biceps tendon surgical repair is prone to selection,

184   reporting, and observer bias. The use of publicly available data limits the capability to define

185   injury severity and the specific surgical procedure and technique performed. Details such as past

186   medical and surgical history, surgical technique, and rehab protocols were not available for

187   collection. Additionally, the sample analyzed in this study may underrepresent the true number

188   of cases that occurred over this 20-year period due to the nature of data collection using publicly

189   available information. The time to return to sport reported in this study is largely dependent on

190   the point in the season at which the injury occurred, making it difficult to draw conclusions from

191   this information. We could not control for potential cofounders including concomitant injuries,

192   trades, personal obligations, coaching changes, or changes in offensive and defensive systems

193   that may have impacted both the case and control cohorts. We must stress that these factors

194   likely confound the findings of decreased post-injury career length and games per season

195   reported in our study, and these results should be interpreted with caution. Furthermore, we

196   could not control for compliance with treatment and rehab protocols. Additional limitations

197   include incomplete follow-up and career length analysis for players still in the NFL. Lastly, we

198   are unable to evaluate offensive linemen with performance scoring.

199

200   Conclusions

201          In this study, we aimed to determine whether surgical repair of distal biceps tendon

202   ruptures in National Football League players would lead to a decrease in post-injury performance

203   and to define return to sport, post-injury career length, and games played per season following

204   injury. In our analysis, 84% of NFL players were able to return to sport following distal biceps




                                                                                                           9
       Distal Biceps Ruptures in NFL Athletes


205   tendon surgical repair. Surgical repair of the distal biceps did not lead to a decrease in

206   performance when compared to the player’s pre-injury performance and control-matched peers,

207   in those athletes that were able to return to play. NFL players who underwent surgical repair of

208   the distal biceps tendon played fewer games per season compared with matched controls,

209   although this finding is likely influenced by a number of factors we could not control for. Players

210   sustaining this injury are unlikely to have a clinically significant decrease in their post-injury

211   career length relative to their peers.

Most players returned to play, the re-injury rate was low, and most reported good knee function years later.",
   "tldr": "Most NCAA Division I football players in this series returned to play after hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction, and few re-injured their knee. Mean Tegner-Lysholm scores were high at a follow-up of about eight years.",
   "methods": "Medical records of male varsity football players who had quadrupled hamstring ACL reconstruction by one surgeon from 2001 to 2016 were reviewed. Return to play, re-injury and eligibility used were taken from institutional records, and a survey provided Tegner-Lysholm scores, with t tests used for comparisons.",
   "findings": "Of 34 players, 29 (85.3%) returned to play after a mean of 318 days, and 2 of those 29 (6.9%) re-injured their knee, both running backs. Players with eligibility remaining used 79.5% of it, and the mean Tegner-Lysholm score was 90.7 plus or minus 14.2 among 33 respondents. Players with multiligament injuries did not differ significantly from isolated ACL injuries in time to return (348 vs 273 days, P=0.709).",
   "limitations": "The study is retrospective, has no comparison arm, and includes a heterogeneous group of positions in a small sample. The Abstract gives multiligament return times (306, 353 and 324 days) that differ from the Results (348 vs 273 days), so the Results were used here, and the Discussion calls the 85.3% return 'the following season' while Results count any return with a mean of 318 days.",
   "practicalImplications": "In this series, hamstring autograft was followed by return to play in most players and a low re-injury rate, so it is a reasonable option to consider in collegiate football players. Because there was no comparison group, the study does not show that hamstring grafts are as safe as patellar tendon grafts. About one in four players needed a second procedure on the same knee, which should be part of counselling.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance staff can expect many collegiate players to use most of their remaining eligibility after hamstring-graft reconstruction, with 25 of 30 eligible players playing again. The 26.5% rate of later ipsilateral knee procedures suggests that monitoring knee function over the career is worthwhile. The study does not measure strength or performance outcomes after return.",
   "rtp": "The mean 318-day return (range 115 to 628 days) and the 85% return rate can inform expectations for collegiate football players after hamstring-graft reconstruction. Return was based on a single surgeon's clearance criteria, including 80% isokinetic strength, so the timeline should not be transferred to other protocols without checking them."
 }

 59   Introduction

60

61   Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury in elite football players is a common and devastating injury. The goal of

62   surgical intervention on ACL injuries is to restore stability of the knee and allow players to return to play (RTP) at

63   their previous level of performance. From 1987 to 2000, 8% of all 5047 players attending the NFL combine had a

64   history of ACL injury and 6% had a subsequent reconstruction.1 According to Dragoo et al, the overall incidence

65   rate of ACL injuries in NCAA football players from 2004-2009 was 1.42 per 10,000 games or practices.2 A recent

66   study by Daruwalla et al. reports that about 20% of NCAA players fail to return to sport after having an ACL

67
                                                                        of
     reconstruction.3 These authors found that players whose ACL was reconstructed with autograft returned to play

68
                                                                 ro
     more often than those whose ACL was reconstructed with allograft. They did not find any difference between the

69
                                                           -p
     types of autograft used for reconstruction, however 90% of the grafts were BTB vs only 10% QH.

70                                                  re
             Traditionally, bone-patella tendon-bone (BTB) grafts have been the gold standard of graft choice in elite

71                                          lP
     athletes. In a 2008 survey, Shrock et al found that NFL team physicians reported using BTB in 87% of their ACL

72

73
                                    na
     reconstructions. That reported preference rose to 97% in 2016. Zero out of 29 reported using hamstring

     autograft.4 Of 49 ACL tears occurring in NFL athletes from 2001-2006, 47 were reconstructed using BTB and 2

74
                             ur
     using QH.5 Carver et al surveyed 100 NCAA Division I team physicians which revealed a similar trend with

75                   Jo
     21% of surgeons using QH in 2008 and only 12% in 2016. With regards to BTB, the usage was 67% and 83% in

76   2008 and 2016, respectively.6 Despite this trend, a paucity of evidence exists showing BTB is a superior option

77   when compared to quadrupled hamstring (QH) autograft in elite athletes and more specifically American football

78   players. With regards to all comers and not just elite football players, Kaeding et al studied 2488 patients and

79   demonstrated a 4.6% reinjury rate with QH graft at 2 year follow-up compared to 3.2% reinjury with BTB7. Two

80   very large 2014 studies from Scandinavia and Norway of 45,998 and 12,643 patients, respectively, found a

81   statistically significant lower risk of revision with BTB grafts vs QH8,9. These studies may contribute to the

82   increased trend of BTB being the most oft-used graft in elite athletes.

83           A graft that can withstand the rigors of elite football performance is of utmost importance. Graft rupture

84   is not uncommon, with 12.3% of all NFL ACL injuries occurring in previously reconstructed knees.10 Lai et al

                                                                                                                          3
 85    performed a meta-analysis of graft re-injury rate in elite athletes including football players undergoing ACL

86    reconstruction and found a rate of 5.2%.11 The ultimate timing of return to play (RTP) is defined by a period of

87    time to allow the graft to heal along with an assessment of the athlete’s strength, proprioception and kinematics.

88    Shrock et al found that the most common time NFL team physicians allowed RTP was 7 to 9 months. In this

89    study, only 14% of surgeons allowed a return before 6 months.4 While both QH and BTB require adequate time

90    to undergo “ligamentization” (a process where the graft initially breaks down and then remodels into a ligament

91    with creeping substitution12 ), a soft tissue only graft like QH also needs to adhere to the femoral and tibial tunnels

92    by forming a fibrovascular scar. It has been found that soft tissue grafts incorporate into their bony tunnels more

93
                                                                          of
      slowly than BTB. 13 For this reason, most surgeons support a BTB graft in elite football players as it allows for

94    bone to bone healing.

102           The purpose of this study was to examine the outcomes of ACL reconstruction using quadrupled

103   hamstring (QH) autograft in a cohort of National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) Division I football

104   players. We hypothesized that the results of this study in a cohort of athletes who had QH reconstruction are

105   similar to historical numbers for athletes undergoing predominantly BTB ACL reconstruction.

108   Institutional review board approval was obtained for this study and all athletes provided informed consent prior to

139             Return to play was defined as actual game play in an official NCAA or professional game after ACL

140   reconstruction. Eligibility remaining was determined based on the number of potential games a player can play in

142   sustained an ACL rupture in the midseason of his freshman year, the potential games remaining would have been

      semitendinosus and gracilis were harvested. The tendons were then prepped by stripping all muscle and

154   tibial tunnel was drilled using a tibial guide placed through the anteromedial portal. The femoral tunnel was then

155   drilled using a trans-tibial technique with the knee in 80 degrees of flexion. The tunnel size was matched to the

156   diameter of the graft. The graft was then passed in a retrograde fashion through both tunnels using a proprietary

157   industry device and then fixated on the femoral side using a Bio-Transfix™ (Athrex; Naples, FL) bioabsorbable

158   crosspin device. This device is preferred by the senior surgeon due to a high load-to-failure as well as minimal

159   graft elongation16. The tibial side was then secured using a BioComposite Interference Screw (Arthrex; Naples,

 "id": "Q77",
 "sourceFile": "Return to play and recurrence after calf muscle strain injuries in elite Australian football players.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text, 'Return to Play and Recurrence After Calf Muscle Strain Injuries in Elite Australian Football Players', matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Case-control Study",
 "primaryDomain": "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport",
 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Registry study of 149 MRI-confirmed calf muscle strain injuries (114 index, 35 recurrent) in elite Australian Football League players over four seasons (2014 to 2017), analysed with Kaplan-Meier, log-rank and Cox regression. Injuries with severe aponeurotic disruption (AD) on MRI took 31.3 days to return to play, compared with 19.4 days for injuries with no AD (P=.003), and a running-related mechanism was independently associated with a longer return (adjusted HR 0.59, P=.02). Older age (adjusted HR 1.1) and a previous calf strain (adjusted HR 6.7) were associated with recurrence within two seasons, while index MRI findings were not.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Registry data from a single league with no uninjured comparison group, and club staff were not blinded to MRI results. Recurrence analyses rest on 35 recurrent injuries (19 early), and the return-to-play period was censored at season end, so the timing estimates are conditional on the data collected.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read the MRI-based return-to-play timelines as individual prognosis, but the group means have wide spread (SD about 11 to 13 days) and the study shows that MRI findings did not predict recurrence.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2020,
   "citation": "Green B, Lin M, McClelland JA, Semciw AI, Schache AG, Rotstein AH, et al. Return to Play and Recurrence After Calf Muscle Strain Injuries in Elite Australian Football Players. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020:1-10.",
   "doi": "10.1177/0363546520959327",
   "abstract": "This study used Australian Football League registry data on calf muscle strains to examine whether clinical and MRI findings were associated with time to return to play and with recurrence. A running-related mechanism and aponeurotic disruption on MRI were linked to longer return to play, while older age and prior calf or ankle injury were linked to recurrence, and index MRI findings were not.",
   "tldr": "In elite Australian Football players, calf strains with aponeurotic disruption on MRI and running-related mechanisms took longer to return to play. Recurrence was better predicted by age and prior calf injury than by the index MRI.",
   "methods": "Clinical and MRI data on 149 calf muscle strain injuries were collected in the AFL Soft Tissue Injury Registry from 2014 to 2017. Two blinded radiologists classified MRI findings, and return to play, functional progression and recurrence within two seasons were analysed using Kaplan-Meier curves, Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis tests, and Cox regression.",
   "findings": "Injuries with severe AD took 31.3 plus or minus 12.6 days to return to play, compared with 19.4 plus or minus 10.8 days with no AD (P=.003). A running-related mechanism was associated with longer return across all injuries (adjusted HR 0.59, P=.02), and AD was associated with longer return for soleus injuries (adjusted HR 0.6, P=.025). Older age (adjusted HR 1.1, P=.013) and a previous calf strain (adjusted HR 6.7, P=.002) were associated with recurrence, while index MRI findings were not.",
   "limitations": "The study has no uninjured comparison group and relies on registry data, with club staff not blinded to MRI results. Recurrent injuries were few (35 overall, 19 early), so the recurrence and subgroup estimates are imprecise, and the mechanism categories overlap. The authors also note that MRI may miss some structural damage, so injuries without visible AD may still have longer recovery.",
   "practicalImplications": "For soleus and other calf strains with visible aponeurotic disruption, or running-related mechanisms, planning should allow for a longer return to play than for injuries without these features. Players with a previous calf strain or older age may carry a higher risk of recurrence, which should shape rehabilitation and return planning. Index MRI findings alone should not be used to predict recurrence.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance staff can use the longer return-to-full-training times for soleus strains with AD to set expectations for training reintroduction. Older players and those with prior calf strains may warrant closer attention during return to running, but the study did not test any monitoring method.",
   "rtp": "Mean return-to-play times were 19.4 days with no AD and 31.3 days with severe AD, with wide spread, so the figures are group benchmarks rather than individual predictions. The study does not validate functional criteria for clearance, and the timelines come from one league, so they should not be applied to other sports without checking."
 }
}

1	Return to Play and Recurrence
2	After Calf Muscle Strain Injuries
3	in Elite Australian Football Players
4	Brady Green,*y PT, MExSc, Monica Lin,z MBBS, FRANZCR, Jodie A. McClelland,y PT, PhD,
5	Adam I. Semciw,y§ PT, GradCert (Epidemiology), PhD, Anthony G. Schache,y PT, PhD,
6	Andrew H. Rotstein,z MBBS, FRANZCR, Jill Cook,y PT, PhD, and Tania Pizzari,y PT, PhD
7	Investigation performed at La Trobe Sport and Exercise Medicine Research Centre,
8	La Trobe University, Victoria, Australia
9	
10	Background: Calf muscle strain injuries (CMSI) are prevalent in sport, but information about factors associated with time to return
11	to play (RTP) and recurrence is limited.
12	Purpose: To determine whether clinical and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data are associated with RTP and recurrence
13	after CMSI.
14	Study Design: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3.
15	Methods: Data of 149 CMSI reported to the Soft Tissue injury Registry of the Australian Football League were explored to eval-
16	uate the impact of clinical data and index injury MRI findings on RTP and recurrence. Clinical data included age, previous injury
17	history, ethnicity, and the mechanism of injury.
18	Results: Irrespective of the anatomical location, players with CMSI with severe aponeurotic disruption (AD) took longer to RTP
19	than players with CMSI with no AD: 31.3 6 12.6 days vs 19.4 6 10.8 days (mean 6 SD; P = .003). A running-related mechanism of
20	injury was associated with a longer RTP period for CMSI overall (adjusted hazard ratio [AHR], 0.59; P = .02). The presence of AD
21	was associated with a longer RTP period for soleus injuries (AHR, 0.6; P = .025). Early recurrence (ie, 2 months of the index
22	injury) was associated with older age (AHR, 1.3; P = .001) and a history of ankle injury (AHR, 3.9; P = .032). Older age (AHR,
23	1.1; P = .013) and a history of CMSI (AHR, 6.7; P = .002) increased the risk of recurrence within 2 seasons. The index injury
24	MRI findings were not associated with risk of recurrence.
25	Conclusion: A running-related mechanism of injury and the presence of AD on MRI were associated with a longer RTP period.
26	Clinical rather than MRI data best indicate the risk of recurrent CMSI.
27	Keywords: calf injury; muscle strain; MRI; soleus; gastrocnemius; return to play

Return to Play and Recurrence
After Calf Muscle Strain Injuries
in Elite Australian Football Players
Brady Green,*y PT, MExSc, Monica Lin,z MBBS, FRANZCR, Jodie A. McClelland,y PT, PhD,
Adam I. Semciw,y§ PT, GradCert (Epidemiology), PhD, Anthony G. Schache,y PT, PhD,
Andrew H. Rotstein,z MBBS, FRANZCR, Jill Cook,y PT, PhD, and Tania Pizzari,y PT, PhD
Investigation performed at La Trobe Sport and Exercise Medicine Research Centre,
La Trobe University, Victoria, Australia

Background: Calf muscle strain injuries (CMSI) are prevalent in sport, but information about factors associated with time to return
to play (RTP) and recurrence is limited.
Purpose: To determine whether clinical and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data are associated with RTP and recurrence
after CMSI.
Study Design: Case-control study; Level of evidence, 3.
Methods: Data of 149 CMSI reported to the Soft Tissue injury Registry of the Australian Football League were explored to eval-
uate the impact of clinical data and index injury MRI findings on RTP and recurrence. Clinical data included age, previous injury
history, ethnicity, and the mechanism of injury.
Results: Irrespective of the anatomical location, players with CMSI with severe aponeurotic disruption (AD) took longer to RTP
than players with CMSI with no AD: 31.3 6 12.6 days vs 19.4 6 10.8 days (mean 6 SD; P = .003). A running-related mechanism of
injury was associated with a longer RTP period for CMSI overall (adjusted hazard ratio [AHR], 0.59; P = .02). The presence of AD
was associated with a longer RTP period for soleus injuries (AHR, 0.6; P = .025). Early recurrence (ie, 2 months of the index
injury) was associated with older age (AHR, 1.3; P = .001) and a history of ankle injury (AHR, 3.9; P = .032). Older age (AHR,
1.1; P = .013) and a history of CMSI (AHR, 6.7; P = .002) increased the risk of recurrence within 2 seasons. The index injury
MRI findings were not associated with risk of recurrence.
Conclusion: A running-related mechanism of injury and the presence of AD on MRI were associated with a longer RTP period.
Clinical rather than MRI data best indicate the risk of recurrent CMSI.
Keywords: calf injury; muscle strain; MRI; soleus; gastrocnemius; return to play

                                                                                         stretch-shortening cycle during dynamic activities, and the

                                                                                         (where CMSI often manifest) can be expected to experience

                                                                                         during jumping, 5.2-times body weight during submaximal
                                                                                         vertical hopping, and up to 12.5-times body weight during
                                                                                         running at 6 m/s.29 Given the enormity of these loads and
                                                                                         the critical role of the aponeuroses for optimal muscle–ten-
                                                                                         don unit function, it is logical that soleus injuries with AD

 "decision": "INCLUDE",

 "domains": ["Rehabilitation & Return to Sport", "Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Performance"],
 "sports": ["Other Sport"],
 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary": "Registry study of 149 MRI-confirmed calf muscle strain injuries (114 index, 35 recurrent) in elite Australian Football League players over four seasons (2014 to 2017), analysed with Kaplan-Meier, log-rank and Cox regression. Injuries with severe aponeurotic disruption (AD) on MRI took 31.3 days to return to play, compared with 19.4 days for injuries with no AD (P=.003), and a running-related mechanism was independently associated with a longer return (adjusted HR 0.59, P=.02). Older age (adjusted HR 1.1) and a previous calf strain (adjusted HR 6.7) were associated with recurrence within two seasons, while index MRI findings were not.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Registry data from a single league with no uninjured comparison group, and club staff were not blinded to MRI results. Recurrence analyses rest on 35 recurrent injuries (19 early), and the return-to-play period was censored at season end, so the timing estimates are conditional on the data collected.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read the MRI-based return-to-play timelines as individual prognosis, but the group means have wide spread (SD about 11 to 17 days), AD stayed independently linked to return time only for soleus injuries, and MRI findings did not predict recurrence.",
 "paper": {
   "year": 2020,
   "citation": "Green B, Lin M, McClelland JA, Semciw AI, Schache AG, Rotstein AH, et al. Return to Play and Recurrence After Calf Muscle Strain Injuries in Elite Australian Football Players. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2020.",
   "doi": "10.1177/0363546520959327",
   "abstract": "This study used Australian Football League registry data on calf muscle strains to examine whether clinical and MRI findings were associated with time to return to play and with recurrence. A running-related mechanism and aponeurotic disruption on MRI were linked to longer return to play, while older age and prior calf or ankle injury were linked to recurrence, and index MRI findings were not.",
   "tldr": "In elite Australian Football players, calf strains with aponeurotic disruption on MRI and running-related mechanisms took longer to return to play. Recurrence was better predicted by age and prior calf injury than by the index MRI.",
   "methods": "Clinical and MRI data on 149 calf muscle strain injuries were collected in the AFL Soft Tissue Injury Registry from 2014 to 2017. Two blinded radiologists classified MRI findings, and return to play, functional progression and recurrence within two seasons were analysed using Kaplan-Meier curves, Mann-Whitney and Kruskal-Wallis tests, and Cox regression.",
   "findings": "Injuries with severe AD took 31.3 plus or minus 12.6 days to return to play, compared with 19.4 plus or minus 10.8 days with no AD (P=.003). A running-related mechanism was associated with longer return across all injuries (adjusted HR 0.59, P=.02), and AD was associated with longer return for soleus injuries (adjusted HR 0.6, P=.025), but not for all calf strains once adjusted (P=.11). Older age (adjusted HR 1.1, P=.013) and a previous calf strain (adjusted HR 6.7, P=.002) were associated with recurrence, while index MRI findings were not.",
   "limitations": "The study has no uninjured comparison group and relies on registry data, with club staff not blinded to MRI results. Recurrent injuries were few (35 overall, 19 early), so the recurrence and subgroup estimates are imprecise, and the mechanism categories overlap. The authors also note that MRI may miss some structural damage, so injuries without visible AD may still have longer recovery.",
   "practicalImplications": "For soleus strains with visible aponeurotic disruption, and for calf strains with running-related mechanisms, planning should allow for a longer return to play than for injuries without these features. Players with a previous calf strain or older age may carry a higher risk of recurrence, which should shape rehabilitation and return planning. Index MRI findings alone should not be used to predict recurrence.",
   "athleteDev": "Performance staff can use the longer return-to-full-training times for soleus strains with AD to set expectations for training reintroduction. Older players and those with prior calf strains may warrant closer attention during return to running, but the study did not test any monitoring method.",
   "rtp": "Mean return-to-play times were 19.4 days with no AD and 31.3 days with severe AD, with wide spread, so the figures are group benchmarks rather than individual predictions. The study does not validate functional criteria for clearance, and the timelines come from one league, so they should not be applied to other sports without checking."
 },

     "paper.findings, practicalImplications, synthesisCaution: AD was independently associated with RTP only for soleus injuries (Table 3 All CMSI AD multivariable '0.72 (0.5-1.1) .11'; soleus '0.6 (0.4-0.9) .025')",
     "synthesisCaution: SD range 11 to 13 -> 11 to 17 days (mild AD '26.7 6 16.8 days')"
   ],

 }
}

13	 "audiences": ["Sports Medicine", "Rehabilitation", "Performance", "Research & Analytics"],
14	 "sports": ["American Football"],
15	 "populations": ["Professional / Elite", "Injured Athletes"],
16	 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective cohort of 63 NFL wide receivers, tight ends, running backs, defensive backs and linebackers with an Achilles tendon rupture repaired between the 2009-2010 and 2015-2016 seasons, of whom 36 (57.1%) returned to play in at least one game. Return rates were highest for tight ends (71%) and linebackers (70%) and lowest for wide receivers (38%) and running backs (40%), with a mean of 12.6 months to return. The authors report that matched controls outperformed returning players before and after injury, and that returning players declined in all categories, although in Table 3 the only significant within-group change for returning players was in passes defended (P=.0306).",
17	 "screeningLimitations": "Built from public press releases and injury reports, with concomitant injuries not recorded, a small sample split across five position groups, and matched controls who were a frame of reference rather than a true control. Several of the authors' statements about significant performance declines do not match the Table 3 P values.",
18	 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read the position return rates as a prediction of a given player's career, but the study shows that returning players were already more experienced before injury and the authors' claim of broad post-injury decline is not fully supported by the tables.",
19	 "paper": {
20	   "year": 2021,
21	   "citation": "Barton D, Manoharan A, Khwaja A, Sorenson J, Taylor M. Return to Play Following Achilles Tendon Rupture in NFL Players Based on Position. Foot & Ankle Specialist. 2021.",
22	   "doi": "10.1177/19386400211040351",
23	   "abstract": "This retrospective cohort study examined return to play and pre- and post-injury performance in NFL skill-position and linebacker players after Achilles tendon rupture and repair. Just over half of the players returned to at least one game, with rates varying by position, and returning players had more pre-injury games than those who did not.",
24	   "tldr": "About 57 percent of NFL skill-position and linebacker players in this series returned to at least one game after Achilles repair, with tight ends and linebackers highest and wide receivers and running backs lowest. Players who returned were more experienced before injury than those who did not.",
25	   "methods": "NFL injury reports and team rosters from the 2009-2010 to 2015-2016 seasons were used to identify players with Achilles tendon rupture and primary repair. Return to play was defined as playing in at least one NFL game after repair, and each returning player was matched to a same-position control from the same team, with pre- and post-injury statistics compared using paired and unpaired t tests.",
26	   "findings": "Of 63 players, 36 (57.1%) returned to play, with rates of 71% for tight ends, 70% for linebackers, 62% for defensive backs, 40% for running backs and 38% for wide receivers. Returning players had more career games than non-returners (78.3 vs 25.4 for offensive players, P=.0072; 93.6 vs 33.1 for defensive players, P=.0043). In the returning group, passes defended fell from 5.04 to 2.79 (P=.0306), and other categories showed no significant within-group change in Table 3.",
27	   "limitations": "The study is retrospective and built from public data, with concomitant injuries and surgical technique not recorded and small position groups that limit comparisons. The authors state that returning players declined in all categories, but Table 3 shows only one significant within-group change, and the Results give P values for tackles and fumbles that appear in the control column. The Discussion's reported RTP rate of 58% and its claim that tight ends had the longest time to return (14.33 months) differ from the Results (57% and 11.25 months).",
28	   "practicalImplications": "Expected return after Achilles repair varies by position in this NFL series, with wide receivers and running backs returning less often, so position demands should be considered when counselling players. Players who returned had more career games and starts before injury, which suggests that established players had better odds of returning. Clinicians should not assume a full return to pre-injury performance, since the only significant within-group change was a fall in passes defended.",
29	   "athleteDev": "Performance staff can use the reported position return rates and the mean 12.6-month return to plan roster and workload decisions for players returning from Achilles repair. The one significant performance change in returning defensive players (passes defended) suggests monitoring of position-specific skills after return, but the study does not test any training programme.",
30	   "rtp": "Use the position-specific return rates (38% to 71%) and the mean time to return of 12.6 months as group benchmarks, not individual predictions. The return criterion here was a single NFL game, and the study cannot show whether any rehabilitation or operative technique changes that outcome."
31	 }
32	}

 "evidenceSummary": "Retrospective cohort of 63 NFL wide receivers, tight ends, running backs, defensive backs and linebackers with an Achilles tendon rupture repaired between the 2009-2010 and 2015-2016 seasons, of whom 36 (57.1%) returned to play in at least one game. Return rates were highest for tight ends (71%) and linebackers (70%) and lowest for wide receivers (38%) and running backs (40%), with a mean of 12.6 months to return.    "abstract": "This retrospective cohort study examined return to play and pre- and post-injury performance in NFL skill-position and linebacker players after Achilles tendon rupture and repair. Players who returned were more experienced before injury than those who did not.",
   "methods": "NFL injury reports and team rosters from the 2009-2010 to 2015-2016 seasons were used to identify players with Achilles tendon rupture and primary repair. Return to play was defined as playing in at least one NFL game after repair, and each returning player was matched to a same-position control from the same team, with pre- and post-injury statistics compared using paired and unpaired t tests.",
   "findings": "Of 63 players, 36 (57.1%) returned to play, with rates of 71% for tight ends, 70% for linebackers, 62% for defensive backs, 40% for running backs and 38% for wide receivers. In the returning group, passes defended fell from 5.04 to 2.79 (P=.0306) and other categories showed no significant within-group change, while against controls the returning players had fewer receptions per game (P=.01), tackles (P=.0069) and passes defended (P=.0452).",

16	 "evidenceSummary": "Level IV case series of NFL players treated by two surgeons at one centre over more than 25 years, with 47 ACL reconstructions (41 primary, 6 revision) in 43 players. Return to game play after primary reconstruction was 73%, and return to previous participation (a new, broader definition) was 87.8%. Age of 25 years or younger was the only independent predictor of return to previous participation (adjusted OR 10.8, P=.02), and offensive position and draft rounds 1 to 4 were associated with more seasons played after surgery.",
17	 "screeningLimitations": "Single-centre series from two surgeons who also made return decisions, with a new return definition that the authors themselves propose and did not validate. 18	 "synthesisCaution": "Staff may read the 87.8% return rate as a general success rate for NFL ACL surgery, but it uses a broader definition than game return, comes from one centre and two surgeons, and the age and position findings are small-sample associations.",

20	   "year": 2020,
21	   "citation": "Khair M, Riboh J, Solis J, Maurer J, Brown JB, Vandermeer RD, et al. Return to Play Following Isolated and Combined Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction: 25+ Years of Experience Treating National Football League Athletes. Orthop J Sports Med. 2020;8(10):2325967120959004.",
22	   "doi": "10.1177/2325967120959004",
23	   "abstract": "This case series reports two surgeons' experience treating NFL players with ACL injuries over more than 25 years, using both the standard return-to-game-play definition and a broader return-to-previous-participation definition. Return to previous participation was higher than return to game play, and age 25 years or younger predicted success.",
24	   "tldr": "Most NFL players in this single-centre series returned to their previous level of participation after ACL reconstruction, and the rate was higher than return-to-game-play figures from earlier series. Players aged 25 or younger were most likely to return.",

Return to game play (one regular-season game) and return to previous participation (same level, cleared by the NFL physical and sustained for at least six weeks) were recorded, and univariate and multivariate logistic and linear regression were used to identify predictors.",
26	   "findings": "Return to game play after primary reconstruction was 73% (27 of 37 knees), and return to previous participation was 87.8% (36 of 41 primary reconstructions). Age 25 years or younger predicted return to previous participation (adjusted OR 10.8, 95% CI 1.4 to 233, P=.02), with 96.2% of players in that group returning compared with 76.2% of older players. Offensive players (adjusted 1.18 more seasons, P=.009) and players drafted in rounds 1 to 4 (adjusted 1.48 more seasons, P=.008) played more seasons after surgery.",
27	   "limitations": "This is a single-centre series with two surgeons who also made return decisions, which may introduce selection bias, and follow-up duration was not recorded. The revision and multiligament groups are very small. The text and abstract differ: the abstract gives 47 players while the Results give 47 reconstructions in 43 players, the abstract gives an overall game-return rate of 67.6% while Table 4 gives 29 of 43 (67.4%), and the abstract's claim that revision and bicruciate-plus-collateral reconstruction lowered return is not significant in Tables 3 and 5 (P=.999 and P=.32).",
28	   "practicalImplications": "For NFL players after ACL reconstruction, age 25 or younger was linked to returning to previous participation, and draft round and offensive position were linked to more seasons played after surgery, so these should be part of counselling. The return rate depends on the definition used, so clinicians should state which definition they are using when comparing outcomes. The study does not support a claim that revision reconstruction or multiligament surgery lowers return with any confidence.",
29	   "athleteDev": "Performance staff can use the 2.6-season average participation after surgery and the higher seasons played by higher draft picks and offensive players as context for long-term planning. The study does not measure strength, speed or other performance outcomes after return.",
30	   "rtp": "The 73% return to game play and 87.8% return to previous participation can serve as group benchmarks for NFL players after primary ACL reconstruction, with the authors' broader definition counting players who returned to their previous level without playing in a game. The study does not show that any rehabilitation protocol changes these rates, and the outcomes come from one centre, so the figures should not be applied to other levels without checking."

11	Investigation performed at The Carrell Clinic, Dallas, Texas, USA

13	Background: The first case series to report on return to play (RTP) in National Football League (NFL) players after primary anterior
14	cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction (ACLR) published an RTP rate of 63%. Other studies that have attempted to estimate RTP
15	after ACLR in these elite athletes have been largely based on secondary sources. This study is the second to report the authors’
16	own results in treating ACL injuries in NFL players spanning a study period of 25þ years.
17	Purpose: To report the senior authors’ experience treating ACL injuries in NFL players as well as revisit the concept of RTP as it is
18	currently used to measure successful surgical outcomes in professional athletes.
19	Study Design: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
20	Methods: A total of 47 NFL players were treated at our institution for knee injuries that included a complete tear of the ACL; of
21	these, 41 were primary ACLR and 6 were revision ACLR. Of the primary ACLRs, 6 were classified as ACL plus additional ligament
22	and 3 were classified as multiligament. Return to game play (RTGP) was defined as returning to play in a regular-season game.
23	Successful return to previous participation (RTPP) was defined as return to a level of participation equal to the level the player had
24	reached before injury. Multivariate analysis was used to assess predictors of successful RTPP.
25	Results: Using the RTGP criteria proposed by prior authors, the RTGP after primary ACLR was 73%. Using our proposed RTPP
26	criteria, 87.8% of players successfully returned to the same level of participation after primary ACLR. RTGP percentage for all NFL
27	players after ACLR (including multiligament injuries) was 67.6%, and the overall RTPP for those patients was 87.8%. In multivariate
28	analysis, age 25 years was predictive of successful RTPP. High draft picks and offensive players played more seasons after
29	primary ACLR. ACL graft rupture occurred in 4.3% of this cohort. Contralateral ACL tear occurred in 8.5%.
30	Conclusion: Regardless of which definition is used to measure a successful outcome after ACLR surgery, the findings of this study
31	suggest that successful return after primary ACLR in NFL athletes is higher than previously reported. While concomitant recon-
32	struction of a single collateral ligament did not affect RTPP, revision ACLR or bicruciate plus collateral ligament reconstruction was
33	associated with a lower RTPP rate. Age 25 years predicted successful RTPP. The risk of a future ACL tear of either knee after
34	index reconstruction was approximately 13%.
35	Keywords: knee ligament injuries; football injuries; athletic rehabilitation; disability evaluation

Original Research


Return to Play Following Isolated and
Combined Anterior Cruciate Ligament
Reconstruction
25þ Years of Experience Treating National Football
League Athletes
Michael Khair,* MD, Jonathan Riboh,† MD, Jaicus Solis,‡§ MD, Jim Maurer,k ATC,
J. Britt Brown,k ATC, Robert D. Vandermeer,* MD, and Daniel E. Cooper,* MD
Investigation performed at The Carrell Clinic, Dallas, Texas, USA

Background: The first case series to report on return to play (RTP) in National Football League (NFL) players after primary anterior
cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction (ACLR) published an RTP rate of 63%. Other studies that have attempted to estimate RTP
after ACLR in these elite athletes have been largely based on secondary sources. This study is the second to report the authors’
own results in treating ACL injuries in NFL players spanning a study period of 25þ years.
Purpose: To report the senior authors’ experience treating ACL injuries in NFL players as well as revisit the concept of RTP as it is
currently used to measure successful surgical outcomes in professional athletes.
Study Design: Case series; Level of evidence, 4.
Methods: A total of 47 NFL players were treated at our institution for knee injuries that included a complete tear of the ACL; of
these, 41 were primary ACLR and 6 were revision ACLR. Of the primary ACLRs, 6 were classified as ACL plus additional ligament
and 3 were classified as multiligament. Return to game play (RTGP) was defined as returning to play in a regular-season game.
Successful return to previous participation (RTPP) was defined as return to a level of participation equal to the level the player had
reached before injury. Multivariate analysis was used to assess predictors of successful RTPP.
Results: Using the RTGP criteria proposed by prior authors, the RTGP after primary ACLR was 73%. Using our proposed RTPP
criteria, 87.8% of players successfully returned to the same level of participation after primary ACLR. RTGP percentage for all NFL
players after ACLR (including multiligament injuries) was 67.6%, and the overall RTPP for those patients was 87.8%. In multivariate
analysis, age 25 years was predictive of successful RTPP. High draft picks and offensive players played more seasons after
primary ACLR. ACL graft rupture occurred in 4.3% of this cohort. Contralateral ACL tear occurred in 8.5%.
Conclusion: Regardless of which definition is used to measure a successful outcome after ACLR surgery, the findings of this study
suggest that successful return after primary ACLR in NFL athletes is higher than previously reported. While concomitant recon-
struction of a single collateral ligament did not affect RTPP, revision ACLR or bicruciate plus collateral ligament reconstruction was
associated with a lower RTPP rate. Age 25 years predicted successful RTPP. The risk of a future ACL tear of either knee after
index reconstruction was approximately 13%.
